audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet Joash reign, temple-repair finance, Hazael tribute, and assassination narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for child-king maturation under Jehoiada, high-place continuity, dedicated-money categories, failed repair system, chest collection, counting and distribution controls, artisan trust, priestly revenue, imperial tribute from sacred treasury, and palace assassination.

verses.restored: In seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash became king, and forty years he reigned in Jerusalem. Name of his mother was Zibiah from Beer-sheba.

modern.text: In the seventh year of Jehu, Joash became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem forty years. His mother’s name was Zibiah; she was from Beersheba.

translation_notes: Joash begins as a rescued child and rules under Jehoiada's instruction. His later authority does not erase the formative control adults exercised around him.

Temple-repair money initially passes through informal priestly relationships, and the repairs remain undone for decades. Sacred status does not remove the need for transparent systems and measurable outcomes.
The chest, joint counting by royal and priestly officials, and direct payment to supervisors and artisans show financial controls replacing an ineffective arrangement.
Trust in work supervisors is praised, but this verse must not be used to reject audits, worker protections, receipts, or modern fiduciary accountability.
Carpenters, builders, masons, stonecutters, and suppliers perform the repair. Their labor, skill, safety, and fair payment belong at the center of the temple story.

Sacred and royal treasures are transferred to Hazael to avert attack. A ruler's survival strategy can preserve a city while also exposing dependence, extortion, and the vulnerability of public resources.
Joash is assassinated by servants. The narrative provides no trial or full motive here; conspiracy and regicide are not accountability systems.
Parallel material in Chronicles differs substantially and requires source-witness audit rather than forced harmonization.
safety_note: Do not use this chapter to excuse clerical financial opacity, unpaid sacred labor, imperial extortion, or assassination. Preserve transparent stewardship, skilled workers' dignity, public accountability, and the distinction between protecting a community and buying a ruler's security with communal treasure.
